Lab 3A

Classification with (regularized) Logistic Regression, and LDA

2026

Getting Started: Loading the Dataset

Before you begin the practical, you need to load the required dataset into R. To ensure a smooth workflow, please follow one of the two options below:

Option 1: Using a Dedicated Folder

Create a specific folder for this assignment and place the dataset file inside it. You can then load the data using the load() function by specifying the correct file path. (Note for Windows users: Please ensure you change all backslashes \ in your copied file path to forward slashes / in R).

   For Mac users, your path will look like this:

load("/Users/your_username/Documents/folder_name/dataset_name.RData")

   For Windows users, your path will look like this:

load("C:/Users/your_username/Documents/folder_name/dataset_name.RData")

Option 2: Using an R Project

Create an R Project (.Rproj) for this assignment and store the dataset directly within that project folder. Make sure to open RStudio by double-clicking the .Rproj file. This automatically sets your working directory, allowing you to load the dataset directly without a long path:

load("dataset_name.RData")

Note for this specific lab: While the above options outline the standard workflow for local files, you do not need to download or load a .RData file for this specific lab. Today, we will access our data directly through the kernlab package using the data(“spam”) command.

In this lab you train models to classify emails as either spam or non-spam based 57 features of the email. The data set for this lab is spam from the package kernlab. The variable type contains the classifications. Other packages you need are MASS, glmnet, caret and pRoc.

The Spam dataset

The dataset spam from the package kernlab contains information about emails and whether they are classified as spam or non-spam.

  • The dataset contains 4601 emails.
  • Each email is described by 57 numeric features.
  • These features measure properties of the email such as:
    • frequency of specific words (e.g. free, money, remove)
    • frequency of special characters (e.g. !, $)
    • statistics related to capital letters.

The response variable type indicates whether the email is:

  • "spam" – unsolicited or unwanted email
  • "nonspam" – legitimate email

The goal of this lab is to build classification models that can predict whether an email is spam based on these features.

Data exploration

  1. Load the necessary packages, and load the spam data in workspace with the function data(). Check its help file for the description of the data.

    Hint: If you haven’t installed kernlab or pROC yet, you will need to run install.packages() first. Use ?spam to view the documentation.

Show Answer 
library(kernlab)
library(MASS)
library(glmnet)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(pROC)
library(caret)
data("spam")


  1. Display the boxplots of the standardized features (so exclude the variable type). What does these plots tell you about the distributions of the features?

    Hint: Use the scale() function to standardize the features before plotting. Look at the range and the dots representing outliers.

Show Answer 
boxplot(scale(spam[, -58]), cex = .3, las = 2)

# The scale() function standardizes the features for comparison.
# The resulting boxplots show tightly clustered medians but massive outliers, indicating highly right-skewed distributions.

As you can see the predictors have strongly skewed distributions with many outliers, which motivates the log transformation applied in the next step of the lab.


  1. To reduce the magnitude of the outliers, make the data logspam containing the standardized logarithms of the each feature (add 1 to each feature to avoid taking the log of 0), and plot the the features to check the effects of the transformations on the \(z\)-scores.

    Hint: You can use dplyr functions like mutate and across, or apply the transformation using base R.

Show Answer 
# Applying log(x + 1) transformation shrinks extreme values and reduces skewness.
# Standardizing them afterwards makes the scales comparable across all 57 features.
logspam <- spam %>% 
  mutate(across(-58, ~ scale(log(.x + 1))))

boxplot(logspam[, -58], cex = .5, las = 1)


Data partitioning

We first make a vector to partition the data in a training set consisting of 75% of the data, and a test of 25% of the data.

  1. Set the seed to 10 for reproducibility, and make the vector train consisting of 75% of the row numbers.

    **Hint:* createDataPartition() from the caret package ensures that the proportion of spam/nonspam is balanced between the train and test sets.

Show Answer 
# Setting a seed guarantees we get the exact same random split every time we run the script.
# The train object stores the row indices for the training data (75% of total).
set.seed(10) 
train <- createDataPartition(y = logspam$type, p = .75, list = FALSE)


Model training

We first train the three logistic regression models (one without and two with regularization), and the linear discriminant model.

Logistic regression

  1. Fit the logistic regression model with all 57 features to the training set, and save the object as train_glm.

    Hint: Use the glm() function and specify family = "binomial" for binary classification.

Show Answer 
# Fitting a standard logistic regression model using all features.
# R may throw a warning about fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1, pointing to perfect separation in some features.
train_glm <- glm(type ~ . , family = "binomial", data = logspam[train, ])

The warning glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred implies that one or more features have extreme parameter estimates and standard errors.


  1. Display the parameter estimates with coef(summary(train_glm)), rounded to two decimals, and identify the features with extreme parameters estimates and standard errors.

    Hint: Look down the ‘Estimate’ and ‘Std. Error’ columns for unusually large numbers compared to the rest of the variables.

Show Answer 
# The summary reveals which features drive the separation.
# Variables with enormous estimates and standard errors are suffering from instability (often due to sparsity or multicollinearity).
round(coef(summary(train_glm)), 2)

LASSO and ridge regression

Shrinkage avoids extremely large parameter estimates. The function glmnet() performs both lasso and ridge regression.

  1. Train the logistic regression model with the LASSO and the ridge. Do not forget that argument x requires a matrix as input, and to set the familiy to "binomial". Save the objects as train_lasso and train_ridge.

    Hint: alpha = 1 (the default) fits a LASSO model, while alpha = 0 fits a Ridge model. Convert the predictors using as.matrix().

Show Answer 
# LASSO (alpha = 1) performs variable selection by shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero.
train_lasso <- glmnet(x = as.matrix(logspam[train, -58]), 
                      y = logspam[train, 58], 
                      family = "binomial")
# Ridge (alpha = 0) shrinks coefficients continuously toward zero, but keeps all variables in the model.
train_ridge <- glmnet(x = as.matrix(logspam[train, -58]), 
                      y = logspam[train, 58], 
                      family = "binomial", 
                      alpha = 0)


  1. Plot both objects using the arguments label = TRUE and xvar = "lambda".
    Here, label = TRUE shows the predictor names in the plot, and xvar = "lambda" places the penalty parameter lambda on the x-axis. The plots display the coefficient paths as a function of lambda: as lambda increases, the coefficients are increasingly shrunk toward zero. Which coefficients are most strongly affected by this shrinkage?

    Hint: Look at the lines that start with very high absolute values on the left side of the plot and rapidly drop towards the zero line.*

Show Answer 
# These plots visualize the coefficient paths.
# Notice how LASSO drops features completely out of the model earlier, while Ridge shrinks them asymptotically.
plot(train_lasso, label = TRUE, xvar="lambda")

plot(train_ridge, label = TRUE, xvar="lambda")


  1. Perform a 5-fold cross-validation to determine the optimal value for the shrinkage parameters lambda with cv.glmnet(). Save the objects as train_cv.lasso and train_cv.ridge. Set the seed to 1 for reproducibility.

    Hint: Use the nfolds = 5 argument. cv.glmnet() will automatically test a sequence of lambda values to find the one with the lowest error.*

Show Answer 
# Cross-validation identifies the optimal penalty parameter (lambda) that minimizes out-of-sample deviance.
set.seed(1)
train_cv.lasso <- cv.glmnet(x = as.matrix(logspam[train, -58]), 
                            y = logspam[train, 58], 
                            family = "binomial",
                            nfolds = 5)
train_cv.ridge <- cv.glmnet(x = as.matrix(logspam[train, -58]), 
                            y = logspam[train, 58], 
                            family = "binomial",
                            nfolds = 5,
                            alpha = 0)


  1. Plot the objects train_cv.lasso and train_cv.lasso, and interpret the plots.

    Hint: The dashed vertical lines represent the optimal lambda (minimum error) and the lambda within 1 standard error of the minimum. The y-axis shows the binomial deviance (error measure).

Show Answer 
# The plots display the cross-validated error curve.
# The left dashed line represents lambda.min, offering the best predictive performance.
plot(train_cv.lasso)

plot(train_cv.ridge)


  1. Display the parameter estimates of train_glm, spam.cv.lasso and spam.cv.ridge side-by-side with the function cbind(), rounded to two decimals.

    Hint: coef(train_cv.lasso) automatically extracts the coefficients using the optimal lambda value.

Show Answer 
# Comparing the models highlights the regularization effect.
# LASSO has produced a sparser model (many 0s), while Ridge has reduced the scale of the extreme GLM estimates.
round(
  cbind(
    coef(train_glm), 
    coef(train_cv.lasso), 
    coef(train_cv.ridge)), 
  2)

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)

LDA is a classification method that models the distribution of the predictors within each class. It assumes that the predictors follow a multivariate normal distribution and that all classes share the same covariance matrix. Based on these assumptions, LDA finds a linear combination of the predictors that best separates the classes and uses it to classify new observations.

  1. Perform a linear discriminant analysis on the logspam data. Save the fitted object under an appropriate name.

    Hint:Use lda() from the MASS package. The syntax is similar to standard formula modeling (e.g., grouping can also be handled via formula type ~ .).

Show Answer 
# LDA finds the axis (linear discriminant) that maximizes the separation between spam and nonspam.
train_lda <- lda(x = logspam[train, -58], grouping = logspam[train, 58])


  1. Display and interpret the content of the lda object.

    Hint: The output displays prior probabilities (class baseline frequencies), group means, and the coefficients for the linear combinations (LD1).

Show Answer 
# The output provides the prior probabilities (proportions) of each class.
# Group means show average feature values per class, and LD1 coefficients dictate the final separation rule.
train_lda

Do you agree with the follwing: The prior probabilities show that about 61% of the training emails are nonspam and 39% are spam. The group means indicate how the standardized feature values differ between spam and nonspam emails. Many words associated with spam (e.g., free, money, remove) have higher average values in spam emails, while words more typical of legitimate emails (e.g., hp, george) have higher averages in nonspam emails.

The linear discriminant coefficients (LD1) show how each feature contributes to separating spam from nonspam emails. Features with larger absolute coefficients have a stronger influence on the classification decision.

  1. Plot the fitted object, and interpret its meaning.

    Hint: Passing an lda object directly into plot() will generate histograms or density plots of the discriminant scores.

Show Answer 
# The histogram visualizes how well the LD1 axis separates the two classes.
# Less overlap indicates a more confident classification model.
plot(train_lda)


Model testing

We now evaluate the performance of the three logistic regression models and the LDA model on the test set.

  1. Use the function predict() to obtain predictions for the test data. Consult the help pages for predict.glm and predict.lda to determine the appropriate arguments. Save the predicted values in objects with informative names (e.g., pred_glm, pred_lasso, etc.).

    Hint: For logistic regression (GLM and GLMNET), use type = "response" to output probabilities. predict.lda() returns a list containing multiple elements.

Show Answer 
# We use the models trained on the 75% training set to predict outcomes on the 25% holdout test set.
# For LDA, predict() outputs a list containing predicted classes and posterior probabilities.
pred_glm    <- predict(train_glm, 
                            newdata = logspam[-train, -58], 
                             type = "response")

pred_lasso  <- predict(train_cv.lasso, 
                            newx = as.matrix(logspam[-train, -58]), 
                            type = "response") 

pred_ridge  <- predict(train_cv.ridge, 
                            newx = as.matrix(logspam[-train, -58]), 
                            type = "response") 


pred_lda    <- predict(train_lda, logspam[-train, -58])


  1. Inspect the predicted objects and determine how the predicted class labels can be obtained. For some models, you will need to convert predicted probabilities into the factor levels "nonspam" and "spam", while for others the predicted classes can be extracted directly. Save these factors under appropriate names (e.g. class_glm, class_lasso, etc.).

    Hint: Convert probabilities to classes by applying a logical condition (e.g., > 0.5) and wrapping it in factor() with proper labels. For LDA, extract the $class element.

Show Answer 
# A 0.5 threshold is applied to the logistic models to assign a hard class label.
# The FALSE/TRUE boolean outcomes naturally map to "nonspam" and "spam" via the labels argument.
class_glm   <- factor(pred_glm > .5, 
                         labels = c("nonspam", "spam"))

class_lasso <- factor(pred_lasso > 0.5, 
                             labels = c("nonspam", "spam"))

class_ridge <- factor(pred_ridge > 0.5, 
                             labels = c("nonspam", "spam"))

class_lda   <- pred_lda$class


  1. Display the confusion matrices of the four models, and save them under appropriate names. Recall that a confusion matrix is a table comparing the observed and predicted classes, showing the numbers of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.

    Hint: Use the table() function, comparing the actual test labels with your newly generated class predictions.

Show Answer 
# Creating a helper function to quickly generate cross-tabulations.
# The diagonal represents correct predictions (True Negatives and True Positives).
# Off-diagonals represent misclassifications (False Positives and False Negatives).
conf <- function(est) table(obs = logspam$type[-train], est = est)
conf <- function(est) table(obs = logspam$type[-train], est = est)

(conf_glm   <- conf(class_glm))
##          est
## obs       nonspam spam
##   nonspam     661   36
##   spam         31  422
(conf_lasso <- conf(class_lasso))
##          est
## obs       nonspam spam
##   nonspam     669   28
##   spam         35  418
(conf_ridge <- conf(class_ridge))
##          est

(conf_lda   <- conf(class_lda))

  1. Compute and display the misclassification test error rates of the five models. Recall that the misclassification error rate is the proportion of incorrectly classified observations in the test set, that is, \(1 - \text{accuracy}\).

    Hint: You can calculate accuracy by taking the sum of the diagonal of the confusion matrix and dividing it by the total sum of the matrix.

Show Answer 
# Calculating the ratio of incorrect predictions over the total number of test cases.
# Lower error rates indicate better generalization to unseen data.
miscl <- function(x) 1 - sum(diag(x)) / sum(x)

data.frame(glm   = miscl(conf_glm),
           lasso = miscl(conf_lasso),
           ridge = miscl(conf_ridge),
           lda   = miscl(conf_lda)) %>% 
  round(4) 
##      glm  lasso  ridge    lda
## 1 0.0583 0.0548 0.0609 0.0661


  1. In a single figure, display the ROC curves (in different colors) for the following predicted probabilities:

  • the random variable runif(1150)

  • the lasso model

  • the LDA model

    Interpret the differences between these curves. Recall that the ROC curve shows the trade-off between the true positive rate and the false positive rate across all classification thresholds, and that a curve closer to the top-left corner indicates better classification performance.

    Hint: Use the roc() function from the pROC package. You can plot multiple curves by passing add = TRUE to the subsequent plot() calls.

Show Answer 
# The ROC curve illustrates diagnostic ability across all possible probability thresholds.
# A larger Area Under the Curve (AUC) indicates a stronger ability to distinguish spam from nonspam.
# The random curve (black) runs diagonally, while GLM (blue) and LDA (red) bow towards the top left, showing strong predictive power.
plot(roc(logspam[-train, 58], runif(1150)))
## Setting levels: control = nonspam, case = spam
## Setting direction: controls > cases
plot(roc(logspam[-train, 58], pred_glm), add = T, col="blue")
## Setting levels: control = nonspam, case = spam
## Setting direction: controls < cases
plot(roc(logspam[-train, 58], pred_lda$posterior[, 2]), add = T, col="red")
## Setting levels: control = nonspam, case = spam
## Setting direction: controls < cases


Bonus

  1. Conduct all previous analyses on the original data (i.e. without the log transformations), and compare the misclassification error rates on the test set. Was the log transformation worth the effort?

    Hint: Simply swap logspam for spam in all functions, ensuring you rerun the models from scratch using the un-transformed dataset.

Show Answer 
# Fitting the entire suite of models on the original, un-transformed dataset.
# The resulting error rates can be directly compared to the log-transformed results to evaluate preprocessing impact.

# 1. Fit models
train_glm <- glm(type ~ . , family = "binomial", data = spam[train, ])

train_lasso <- glmnet(x = as.matrix(spam[train, -58]), 
                      y = spam[train, 58], 
                      family = "binomial")

train_ridge <- glmnet(x = as.matrix(spam[train, -58]), 
                      y = spam[train, 58], 
                      family = "binomial", 
                      alpha = 0)

set.seed(1)
train_cv.lasso <- cv.glmnet(x = as.matrix(spam[train, -58]), 
                            y = spam[train, 58], 
                            family = "binomial",
                            nfolds = 5)
train_cv.ridge <- cv.glmnet(x = as.matrix(spam[train, -58]), 
                            y = spam[train, 58], 
                            family = "binomial",
                            nfolds = 5,
                            alpha = 0)

train_lda <- lda(x = spam[train, -58], grouping = spam[train, 58])

# 2. Predict
pred_glm    <- predict(train_glm, 
                            newdata = spam[-train, -58], 
                             type = "response")

pred_lasso  <- predict(train_cv.lasso, 
                            newx = as.matrix(spam[-train, -58]), 
                            type = "response") 

pred_ridge  <- predict(train_cv.ridge, 
                            newx = as.matrix(spam[-train, -58]), 
                            type = "response") 


pred_lda    <- predict(train_lda, spam[-train, -58])

# 3. Evaluate
class_glm   <- factor(pred_glm > .5, 
                         labels = c("nonspam", "spam"))

class_lasso <- factor(pred_lasso > 0.5, 
                             labels = c("nonspam", "spam"))

class_ridge <- factor(pred_ridge > 0.5, 
                             labels = c("nonspam", "spam"))

class_lda   <- pred_lda$class

conf <- function(est) table(obs = spam$type[-train], est = est)

(conf_glm   <- conf(class_glm))

##          est

data.frame(glm   = miscl(conf_glm),

Conclusion

In this lab we studied several classification methods for predicting whether an email is spam or nonspam using the spam dataset. The exploratory analysis showed that many predictors were strongly skewed and contained outliers, which motivated the use of a log transformation.

We then trained and compared standard logistic regression, regularized logistic regression (LASSO and ridge), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The regularized models illustrated how shrinkage can reduce extreme coefficient estimates and improve model stability.

The models were evaluated on a separate test set using confusion matrices, misclassification error rates, and ROC curves. This showed how different classification methods can be compared not only by their predicted class labels, but also by the quality of their predicted probabilities.

Overall, the lab illustrated the full classification workflow: data exploration, preprocessing, model fitting, regularization, prediction, and performance evaluation on unseen data.
